senses.gloss: Forgetful because your thoughts are somewhere else.
examples: My *absentminded* uncle left his keys in the front door again.
I'm getting more *absentminded* every year.
She gave me an *absentminded* nod and kept reading.

position: predicative only — after *run*, *fall* or *get*: *run afoul of the rules*
contrast: In modern American English the word lives almost entirely in *run afoul of* and *fall afoul of*. Never before a noun.

senses.gloss: In trouble with a law, a rule or a person because of what you did.
examples: The company ran *afoul* of federal regulators.
He fell *afoul* of the coach and lost his spot.
Be careful not to run *afoul* of the new parking rules.

position: predicative only — *we're behind*, never *a behind student*
contrast: *Behind* is much more often a preposition (*behind the house*) or an adverb (*stay behind*). Only the 'late' and 'losing' uses after *be* or *get* are adjectival.

senses.gloss: Late with work, payments or a schedule.
examples: We're two weeks *behind* on the project.
They fell *behind* on the rent after he lost his job.
The flight put us *behind* schedule.

senses.gloss: Losing in a game or a contest.
examples: The Cubs were *behind* by three runs in the seventh.
She's still *behind* in the polls, but the gap is closing.

contrast: The noun is two separate words: *goods sold on the black market*. Only the adjective before a noun takes the hyphen.

senses.gloss: Bought or sold illegally, outside the legal market.
examples: Agents seized thousands of *black-market* cigarettes.
*Black-market* prices for the drug tripled last year.
He paid a *black-market* dealer twice what the ticket was worth.

contrast: Also a noun: *We finally got broadband out here*.

senses.gloss: Of an internet connection: high-speed, carrying a lot of data at once.
examples: Half the county still has no *broadband* service.
The town is paying to run *broadband* cable to every farm.
*Broadband* speeds here are slower than the ad promised.

contrast: The first part is the adjective *close* with an /s/ sound, not the verb /kloʊz/. *Closed-minded* is also written and means the same thing.

senses.gloss: Unwilling to listen to new ideas or other opinions.
examples: Don't be so *close-minded* — at least try the food.
He's the most *close-minded* person on the committee.
A *close-minded* teacher can ruin a subject for a kid.

position: both — usually with an adverb: *a properly configured server*

senses.gloss: Set up with particular settings so that it works a particular way.
examples: The laptop comes *configured* for the school network.
A badly *configured* firewall leaves the whole office exposed.
The alarm is *configured* to text me when the door opens.

contrast: Also a noun for a bug: *The kids collect creepy-crawlies in a jar*.

senses.gloss: Giving you the unpleasant feeling that something is crawling on your skin.
examples: The basement has a *creepy-crawly* feel to it.
Spiders make me all *creepy-crawly*.
She told the kids a *creepy-crawly* story around the fire.

position: attributive only — *a cum laude graduate*; after a verb it is an adverb: *she graduated cum laude*
form: Latin — 'with praise'; stronger: *magna cum laude*, *summa cum laude*
contrast: Keep the Latin phrase in two words and never add *-er* or *very*. The higher honors are *magna cum laude* and *summa cum laude*.

senses.gloss: Of a degree or a graduate: awarded with honors.
examples: He's a *cum laude* graduate of Ohio State.
*Cum laude* honors take a 3.5 average here.
She hung her *cum laude* diploma over the desk.

contrast: Much more common as a noun: *The kid is a little daredevil*.

senses.gloss: Recklessly bold, taking dangerous risks for the thrill.
examples: He made his name with *daredevil* stunts on a motorcycle.
Her *daredevil* driving scares everyone in the car.
The show ended with a *daredevil* jump over eight buses.

contrast: *Dispirited* is how the people feel; *dispiriting* is what causes the feeling: *a dispiriting loss left the team dispirited*.

senses.gloss: Having lost hope and energy.
examples: The volunteers went home tired and *dispirited*.
A *dispirited* crowd filed out before the last inning.
She sounded more *dispirited* than angry on the phone.

contrast: Use *dispiriting* for the thing and *dispirited* for the person: *a dispiriting report*, *a dispirited staff*.

senses.gloss: Making you lose hope and energy.
examples: It was a *dispiriting* end to a good season.
The turnout was *dispiriting*, even to the organizers.
Nothing is more *dispiriting* than a job search that goes nowhere.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *she was displeased*
contrast: A formal, slightly cool word — much milder than *angry*. Bosses and judges are *displeased*; friends are just *annoyed*.

senses.gloss: Annoyed or not satisfied, in a controlled, formal way.
examples: The principal was clearly *displeased* with our excuse.
Shareholders are *displeased* at the pace of the layoffs.
She looked *displeased* but said nothing.

senses.gloss: Causing annoyance or dissatisfaction.
examples: The design was *displeasing* to almost everyone on the board.
He has a *displeasing* habit of talking over people.
Nothing about the room was *displeasing*, but nothing charmed us either.

contrast: Also a noun in the plural: *the hospital buys disposables by the case*.

senses.gloss: Made to be thrown away after one use.
examples: The party ran on *disposable* plates and cups.
She packed *disposable* razors for the trip.
*Disposable* diapers fill the trash fast.

senses.gloss: Of money: left over after taxes and bills, free to spend.
examples: Families here have less *disposable* income than they did in 2019.
Teenagers with *disposable* cash drive the whole market.

position: predicative only — *I'm not disposed to argue*
takes: *to*-infinitive — willing; *toward* or *to* + person, after *well* or *kindly* — friendly
contrast: Formal. In the 'friendly' sense it needs *well*, *kindly* or *ill* in front: *well disposed toward the plan*. Do not confuse it with *disposable* (thrown away after use).

senses.gloss: Willing or inclined to do something.
examples: The judge was not *disposed* to grant another delay.
I'd be more *disposed* to help if he'd asked politely.

senses.gloss: Feeling friendly or unfriendly toward someone or something.
examples: The committee seems well *disposed* toward our proposal.
He was kindly *disposed* to every stray that showed up.

senses.gloss: Too large or too small compared with something else.
examples: The fine seems *disproportionate* to the offense.
A *disproportionate* share of the cuts fell on rural schools.
Their spending on travel is *disproportionate*, given the budget.

senses.gloss: Not agreed on — argued over by two or more sides.
examples: Troops are massed along the *disputed* border.
The bill for the repairs is still *disputed*.
He won a *disputed* election by fewer than a thousand votes.

senses.gloss: Making someone unfit or ineligible for a job, a prize or a competition.
examples: A felony conviction is a *disqualifying* factor for this license.
The doctor found no *disqualifying* condition.
For most voters it wasn't a *disqualifying* mistake.

senses.gloss: Making you feel worried or uneasy.
examples: The report makes *disquieting* reading.
There's something *disquieting* about how quiet the street is.
The most *disquieting* part is that nobody noticed for a month.

senses.gloss: Having a bad reputation; not to be trusted or respected.
examples: He borrowed money from a *disreputable* lender.
The bar had the most *disreputable* crowd in town.
Her landlord is *disreputable* but not quite a criminal.

senses.gloss: Showing no respect for someone or something.
examples: Don't be *disrespectful* to your grandmother.
Leaving in the middle of her speech was *disrespectful*.
That was the most *disrespectful* thing he's ever said to a teacher.

ru: мешающий, нарушающий порядок; радикально меняющий рынок

senses.gloss: Interrupting something and stopping it from going normally.
examples: Two *disruptive* students were sent to the office.
The construction has been *disruptive* to the whole block.
Late-night noise is more *disruptive* than she realizes.

senses.gloss: Of a technology or business: changing an industry completely.
examples: Streaming was the most *disruptive* thing to hit the music business.
They pitch every app as *disruptive* innovation.

contrast: *Dissatisfied* means unhappy with what you got; *unsatisfied* means you did not get enough (*an unsatisfied appetite*, *an unsatisfied claim*).

senses.gloss: Not happy with something because it is not good enough.
examples: Customers are *dissatisfied* with the new billing system.
A *dissatisfied* employee will find another job by spring.
The longer she waited, the more *dissatisfied* she got.

contrast: In court reporting, *a dissenting opinion* is the written opinion of a judge who voted the other way.

senses.gloss: Disagreeing with the official or majority view.
examples: Two justices filed a *dissenting* opinion.
There were a few *dissenting* voices at the town meeting.
The board approved it with one *dissenting* vote.

contrast: Far more common as a noun: *The dissidents were released in 1989*.

senses.gloss: Openly opposing an official policy, especially a government's.
examples: *Dissident* writers were published abroad.
The party expelled its *dissident* wing.
She spent six years in a camp for *dissident* activity.

contrast: Often in the understatement *not dissimilar to*, which means 'fairly similar to'.

senses.gloss: Not alike.
examples: Her style is not *dissimilar* to her mother's.
The two engines are more *dissimilar* than they look.
They came from wildly *dissimilar* backgrounds.

contrast: Chemists and food labels prefer *soluble*; *dissolvable* is the everyday word, and the usual one for stitches and tablets.

senses.gloss: Able to be dissolved in a liquid, or to break down inside the body.
examples: The surgeon used *dissolvable* stitches.
These are *dissolvable* tablets — drop one in water.
The packaging is *dissolvable* in hot water.

senses.gloss: Far away in space.
examples: We could see the lights of a *distant* town.
The telescope picks up the most *distant* galaxies.

senses.gloss: Far away in time, in the past or the future.
examples: Retirement still feels *distant*.
In the not too *distant* future, all of this will be automated.

senses.gloss: Related only slightly, in a family.
examples: He's a *distant* cousin on my father's side.
They're *distant* relatives who meet once a decade.

senses.gloss: Cold and unfriendly, or lost in thought.
examples: She's been *distant* with me since the argument.
He had a *distant* look, as if he hadn't heard the question.

contrast: It is about morals and manners, not food: a joke can be *distasteful*, but soup that tastes bad is just *awful*. *Tasteless* is the closer opposite of *tasteful*.

senses.gloss: Unpleasant or offensive, especially to your sense of what is decent.
examples: The ad was *distasteful* and got pulled in a day.
Firing people by email is *distasteful* to most managers.
He found the whole business more *distasteful* the longer it went on.

contrast: *Distinct* means separate or clear; *distinctive* means recognizable as belonging to one person or thing. *Her voice is distinct* = you hear it clearly; *her voice is distinctive* = you know it's hers.

senses.gloss: Clearly separate and different from something else.
examples: Spanish and Portuguese are *distinct* languages.
The job has two *distinct* parts.
Keep your work email *distinct* from your personal one.

senses.gloss: Easily seen, heard or smelled; unmistakable.
examples: There was a *distinct* smell of gas in the hall.
I got the *distinct* impression she wanted us to leave.

contrast: *Distinctive* marks a thing out as its own; *distinguished* means respected and successful. A *distinctive* hat, a *distinguished* professor.

senses.gloss: Easy to recognize because it belongs to one person or thing and nothing else.
examples: The bird has a *distinctive* white stripe on its head.
Her handwriting is *distinctive* — I'd know it anywhere.
Of all their albums, the first has the most *distinctive* sound.

senses.gloss: Able to be told apart from something else, or made out clearly.
examples: The copy is barely *distinguishable* from the original.
In the fog, the shore was hardly *distinguishable*.
The twins were more *distinguishable* once one cut his hair.

senses.gloss: Respected and successful after a long career.
examples: She had a *distinguished* career in public health.
Our guest tonight is the most *distinguished* alumna of the school.

senses.gloss: Looking dignified and impressive, often because of gray hair.
examples: He looks *distinguished* in that gray suit.
A *distinguished* older gentleman held the door for us.

senses.gloss: Pulled or twisted out of its normal shape or sound.
examples: The guitar had a fuzzy, *distorted* sound.
Our faces looked *distorted* in the funhouse mirror.

senses.gloss: Changed so that it gives a false idea of the truth.
examples: The quote appeared in a badly *distorted* form online.
He has a *distorted* picture of what the job involves.

contrast: *Distracted* is the person; *distracting* is the thing: *the noise was distracting, and I got distracted*.

senses.gloss: Unable to pay attention because something has pulled your mind away.
examples: Sorry, I'm *distracted* — my phone won't stop buzzing.
*Distracted* driving causes thousands of crashes a year.
She seemed more *distracted* than usual at dinner.

contrast: Much stronger than *upset* — it is the word for a parent whose child is missing.

senses.gloss: So upset that you cannot think or act normally.
examples: The *distraught* mother begged for help finding her son.
He was *distraught* over the loss of the dog.
She was too *distraught* to finish the sentence.

senses.gloss: Very upset or worried.
examples: Neighbors were *distressed* by the news.
A *distressed* passenger was taken off the plane.

senses.gloss: Of jeans, leather or furniture: made to look worn and old on purpose.
examples: She wore *distressed* jeans and a white tee.
The table has a *distressed* finish.

senses.gloss: In serious financial trouble.
senses.ru: проблемный, находящийся в тяжёлом финансовом положении
examples: The fund buys *distressed* properties cheap.
Several *distressed* banks were sold off that year.

contrast: The thing is *distressing*; the person is *distressed*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel upset or worried.
examples: The video is *distressing* to watch.
It's *distressing* how little anyone knew.
The most *distressing* part was the silence from the hospital.

senses.gloss: Spread out over an area or among people rather than gathered in one place.
examples: The weight is evenly *distributed* across the four legs.
Rainfall is unevenly *distributed* through the year.

senses.gloss: Of a computer system or a team: split across many machines or locations.
examples: They run a *distributed* database across three data centers.
We're a fully *distributed* company with nobody in an office.

senses.gloss: Not willing to trust someone or something.
examples: Voters are *distrustful* of both parties.
Years in the business left him *distrustful*.
She grew more *distrustful* with every broken promise.

contrast: Calling a person *disturbed* with no adverb suggests mental illness, so say *disturbed by the news* when you only mean worried.

senses.gloss: Worried or upset by something.
examples: Parents were *disturbed* by what they saw in the video.
I'm deeply *disturbed* about the direction this is going.

senses.gloss: Having serious mental or emotional problems.
examples: The letters came from a *disturbed* young man.
He works with emotionally *disturbed* teenagers.

contrast: The report is *disturbing*; the reader is *disturbed*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel worried, shocked or upset.
examples: The footage is *disturbing*, so we won't show all of it.
There's a *disturbing* pattern in these numbers.
The most *disturbing* thing is how normal he seemed.

contrast: The *s* is /z/: dis-YOOZD. *Unused* means never used at all; *disused* means used once but not anymore.

senses.gloss: No longer used, and left empty or idle.
examples: Kids broke into the *disused* factory.
The trail follows a *disused* rail line.
They store hay in the *disused* barn.

senses.gloss: Going in different directions, or differing from one another.
examples: The two reports reach wildly *divergent* conclusions.
Their paths grew more *divergent* after college.
His account is *divergent* from everything the witnesses said.

senses.gloss: Made up of many different kinds.
examples: The park protects a *diverse* set of habitats.
Her interests are unusually *diverse*.

senses.gloss: Including people of many races, backgrounds and cultures.
examples: It's the most *diverse* class the school has ever had.
The neighborhood is far more *diverse* than it was in 1990.

senses.gloss: Spread across several different kinds of business, product or investment.
examples: Keep a *diversified* portfolio and don't panic.
The company is more *diversified* than its competitors.
A *diversified* farm survives a bad year for one crop.

senses.gloss: Meant to draw attention away from something more important.
examples: The fire was a *diversionary* tactic while they emptied the safe.
Critics called the hearing a *diversionary* move.
Troops staged a *diversionary* attack on the south road.

contrast: Sense 1 does not grade — nothing is *more divine* than God. Only the informal 'wonderful' sense takes *more* and *most*, and it sounds dated or theatrical.

senses.gloss: Coming from God or belonging to a god.
examples: They believed the king ruled by *divine* right.
The painting shows *divine* light falling on the shepherds.

senses.gloss: Wonderful — an informal, old-fashioned word of praise.
examples: That chocolate cake was *divine*.
Her new apartment is the most *divine* place you've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Able to be divided, especially with nothing left over.
examples: Nine is *divisible* by three.
The land is *divisible* into four equal lots.
Any even number is *divisible* by two.

senses.gloss: Belonging to one division of a company, an army or a sports league.
examples: The *divisional* manager flew in for the meeting.
They clinched the *divisional* title in September.
Each *divisional* office sets its own hours.

contrast: Stress the second syllable and say it with the vowel of *eye*: dih-VY-siv.

senses.gloss: Causing disagreement and splitting people into opposing groups.
examples: Immigration is the most *divisive* issue on the ballot.
His speech was *divisive*, even inside his own party.
Nothing is more *divisive* at a family dinner than politics.

senses.gloss: No longer married, because the marriage was legally ended.
examples: My parents have been *divorced* since I was six.
She's a *divorced* mother of three.
He got *divorced* last spring.

senses.gloss: Completely separated from something, with no connection left.
examples: The plan is *divorced* from reality.
Their pay is entirely *divorced* from performance.

senses.gloss: Feeling as if everything is spinning and you might fall.
examples: I stood up too fast and felt *dizzy*.
The medicine makes her *dizzier* than the illness did.

senses.gloss: Making you feel that way — of heights, speed or a steep rise.
examples: We climbed to a *dizzy* height above the canyon.
Prices rose at a *dizzy* pace all summer.

form: compound — the whole phrase *do it yourself* used as one adjective
contrast: Usually shortened to *DIY*. It is also a noun: *He's into do-it-yourself*.

senses.gloss: Made or done by ordinary people at home instead of by professionals.
examples: The store has a whole *do-it-yourself* aisle.
She followed a *do-it-yourself* guide to tiling the bathroom.
It's a *do-it-yourself* kit, so bring a screwdriver.

form: compound — the phrase *do nothing* used as one adjective

senses.gloss: Lazy or useless because it takes no action — usually said in anger about politicians.
examples: He campaigned against a *do-nothing* Congress.
The council has a *do-nothing* reputation.
They're tired of *do-nothing* leadership at city hall.

form: compound — the phrase *do or die* used as one adjective

senses.gloss: Where you must succeed now or lose everything.
examples: Saturday is a *do-or-die* game for the Jets.
The startup is in a *do-or-die* month.
She went in with a *do-or-die* attitude.

contrast: Informal but common at work. In writing, *feasible* is the formal choice.

senses.gloss: Possible to do, especially in the time or with the money you have.
examples: Two weeks is tight, but it's *doable*.
Break it into *doable* steps.
Cutting ten percent is more *doable* than cutting thirty.

contrast: Americans say DAH-suhl; the British *DOH-syl* is not used here.

senses.gloss: Quiet and easy to control or lead.
examples: The mare is *docile* enough for a beginner.
He expected a *docile* audience and got an angry one.
The older dog is much more *docile* than the puppy.

contrast: In the United States a *doctoral* program leads to a PhD, not to a medical degree.

senses.gloss: Connected with the highest university degree, the doctorate.
examples: She's writing her *doctoral* dissertation on wetlands.
He teaches in the *doctoral* program in economics.
*Doctoral* students get a small stipend.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the official beliefs of a church, a party or a school of thought.
examples: The split was *doctrinal*, not personal.
They argued for years over a small *doctrinal* point.
The seminary teaches the church's *doctrinal* history.

senses.gloss: Of a book or paper: worn, with the corners of the pages folded over.
examples: He carries a *dog-eared* paperback in his coat pocket.
The recipe card is stained and *dog-eared*.
She handed me a *dog-eared* copy of the map.

contrast: The adjective has two syllables, DAW-gid. The past tense of the verb *dog* is one syllable: *Reporters dogged him for weeks* /dɔːɡd/.

senses.gloss: Refusing to give up, however long it takes.
examples: Her *dogged* reporting finally broke the story.
It took *dogged* persistence to get the permit.
He was the most *dogged* investigator on the force.

senses.gloss: Insisting that your beliefs are right and refusing to consider anything else.
examples: He's *dogmatic* about how coffee should be made.
The book takes a *dogmatic* line on diet.
She got more *dogmatic* as the argument went on.

contrast: Informal and a little old-fashioned, and usually said about women. For a man you would say *all dressed up*.

senses.gloss: Dressed up in fancy clothes and makeup for an occasion.
examples: She got all *dolled up* for the reunion.
Why are you so *dolled up* on a Tuesday?
The girls came downstairs *dolled up* and ready for pictures.

senses.gloss: Having the round, curved shape of a dome, or covered by one.
examples: The *domed* roof lets light into the hall.
They play in a *domed* stadium, so rain never matters.
The lid is slightly *domed* so the steam runs off.

senses.gloss: Inside one country, not foreign.
examples: *Domestic* flights leave from Terminal B.
Most of the company's sales are *domestic*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the home and family.
examples: The police were called to a *domestic* dispute.
She handles most of the *domestic* chores.

senses.gloss: Of an animal: kept by people, not wild.
examples: The shelter takes *domestic* animals only.
Cats were *domestic* long before they were pets.

senses.gloss: Of an animal or plant: bred and kept by people instead of living wild.
examples: Horses were *domesticated* thousands of years ago.
A *domesticated* fox still isn't a dog.

senses.gloss: Of a person: happy doing housework and staying home — usually a joke.
examples: Since the baby, he's completely *domesticated*.
My brother is more *domesticated* than I'll ever be.

senses.gloss: Most powerful, most important or most noticeable.
examples: The company is *dominant* in three states.
Oak is the *dominant* tree in these woods.
She was the most *dominant* player in the league that year.

senses.gloss: Of a gene: showing its effect even when only one parent passes it on.
examples: Brown eyes come from a *dominant* gene.
The trait is *dominant*, so half the litter will show it.

contrast: *Dominating* describes a performance or a presence; *domineering* is always an insult about a person who bosses others around.

senses.gloss: Controlling a game, a market or a scene completely.
examples: It was a *dominating* performance from the freshman.
The defense was *dominating* in the second half.

senses.gloss: Standing over everything else and drawing all the attention.
examples: The cathedral is the *dominating* feature of the skyline.
He has a *dominating* presence in any room.

senses.gloss: Trying to control other people and give them orders.
examples: She grew up with a *domineering* stepfather.
He gets *domineering* the moment he's put in charge.
The coach is the most *domineering* man I've ever worked for.

contrast: Also a noun: *She's a Dominican*. Capital *D* always. The same word names the Dominican order of friars.

senses.gloss: From or connected with the Dominican Republic.
examples: We ate at a *Dominican* restaurant in Washington Heights.
*Dominican* players fill half the roster.
Her mother is *Dominican* and her father is Cuban.

position: predicative only — before a noun only in fixed phrases: *a done deal*
comparison: not gradable — but food can be *more done*, *well done*
contrast: Americans say *I'm done* for 'I have finished'. *Well done* on a steak means cooked through; said to a person it is praise.

senses.gloss: Finished; completed.
examples: The laundry is *done*.
Give me ten minutes and I'll be *done*.
Once the paperwork is *done*, you get the keys.

senses.gloss: Of food: cooked enough.
examples: Check whether the chicken is *done* in the middle.
I like my burger more *done* than that.

senses.gloss: Settled and no longer open to change — in *a done deal*.
examples: The merger is a *done* deal.
Don't treat the promotion as *done* until you sign something.

contrast: Informal and never before a noun. It can be a joke about losing a game or serious about dying.

senses.gloss: Certain to fail, be ruined or die.
examples: If the power goes out now, we're *done for*.
Without that contract the shop is *done for*.
One more penalty and they're *done for*.

ru: покончивший (с чем-либо), больше не имеющий дела
takes: *with* + noun or *-ing* — the *with* is part of the phrase
contrast: *Done with a thing* can mean you have simply finished using it; *done with a person* means the relationship is over.

senses.gloss: Finished using or dealing with something, or refusing to deal with it any longer.
senses.ru: закончивший с чем-либо; покончивший с чем-либо
examples: Are you *done with* the scissors?
I'm *done with* apologizing for him.
After that phone call she was *done with* the whole family.

senses.gloss: Certain to fail, suffer or be destroyed.
examples: The plan was *doomed* from the start.
He plays a *doomed* soldier in the film.
Without water the crop is *doomed* to fail.

contrast: As an adverb it usually drops the hyphens: *They went door to door collecting signatures*.

senses.gloss: Going from one house to the next, or delivered from the sender's door to the receiver's.
examples: He worked as a *door-to-door* salesman for two summers.
The campaign relies on *door-to-door* canvassing.
We pay extra for *door-to-door* delivery.

contrast: Informal. Note the spelling with *-e-*: *dopey*, but *dopier* and *dopiest*.

senses.gloss: Sleepy and slow-thinking, usually from medicine or lack of sleep.
examples: The pills leave me *dopey* all morning.
He was still *dopey* from the anesthesia.

senses.gloss: Silly or a little stupid.
examples: He has a *dopey* grin in every photo.
That's the *dopiest* excuse I've heard all week.

senses.gloss: Not active now, but able to become active again.
examples: The volcano has been *dormant* for two centuries.
The virus can stay *dormant* in the body for years.
A *dormant* account gets closed after eighteen months.

senses.gloss: Of a plant or seed: alive but not growing, usually over winter.
examples: Prune the roses while they're *dormant*.
The seeds lie *dormant* until the first warm rain.

form: compound — from the web address ending *.com*
contrast: Also a noun: *a failed dot-com*. It usually points back to the internet boom of the late 1990s.

senses.gloss: Having to do with internet companies, especially those of the late 1990s boom.
examples: He made and lost a fortune in the *dot-com* boom.
Her parents met at a *dot-com* startup in 1999.
The *dot-com* crash emptied half the office park.

contrast: The verb needs *on*: *She dotes on her nephews*. The adjective goes straight before a noun: *a doting aunt*.

senses.gloss: Loving someone so much that you spoil them and see no fault.
examples: Her *doting* grandfather bought her a pony.
He's a *doting* father of three.
She married the most *doting* man in the county.

senses.gloss: Made of or marked with dots.
examples: Sign on the *dotted* line.
She wore a *dotted* blue dress.

senses.gloss: Covered with small things spread here and there.
examples: The hillside is *dotted* with white farmhouses.
The lawn was *dotted* with dandelions by May.

contrast: *Double* is also a verb (*Prices doubled*) and a noun (*a double at the bar*). Before a noun it needs no *of*: *double the price*, not *double of the price*.

senses.gloss: Twice as much, as many or as big.
examples: He earns *double* what I do.
Order a *double* shot if you're driving tonight.

senses.gloss: Made of two similar parts, or having two of something.
examples: The barn has *double* doors at both ends.
Her name has a *double* l in it.

senses.gloss: Meant for two people.
examples: We booked a *double* room with a view.
The guest bed is a *double*, not a queen.

contrast: American spelling has one *l*: *double-barreled*. The British write *double-barrelled*.

senses.gloss: Of a gun: having two barrels.
examples: He keeps a *double-barreled* shotgun in the truck.
The museum has a *double-barreled* cannon out front.

senses.gloss: Doing two things at once, or having two parts.
senses.ru: двойной, двоякий, бьющий с двух сторон
examples: That's a *double-barreled* question — answer one part at a time.
The storm was a *double-barreled* hit of wind and flooding.

senses.gloss: Of a coat or jacket: with two rows of buttons and fronts that overlap.
examples: He wore a navy *double-breasted* blazer.
*Double-breasted* suits came back in style.
She found a *double-breasted* wool coat at the thrift store.

contrast: Also a noun: *He was fired for double-dealing*.

senses.gloss: Cheating people by secretly working for both sides.
examples: They found out about his *double-dealing* partner too late.
It was a *double-dealing* scheme from day one.
She has no patience for *double-dealing* politicians.

senses.gloss: Of a blade: sharp on both sides.
examples: The knife has a *double-edged* blade.
He collects *double-edged* razors.

senses.gloss: Having a good effect and a bad one at the same time.
senses.ru: имеющий две стороны, как палка о двух концах
examples: Fame is a *double-edged* sword.
The tax break is a *double-edged* gift for small towns.

contrast: Nobody really has two joints — it is the everyday word for unusually flexible joints.

senses.gloss: Able to bend your fingers, arms or legs much further than most people.
examples: She's *double-jointed* and can bend her thumb to her wrist.
A *double-jointed* kid in the class could fold herself in half.
Are you *double-jointed*, or does that just not hurt?

senses.gloss: Typed with a full empty line between the lines of text.
examples: Papers must be *double-spaced* and twelve point.
She handed in a *double-spaced* draft with wide margins.
Is the whole thing *double-spaced*, including the notes?

contrast: The *b* is silent: DOWT-fuhl. With a thing as subject it means 'unlikely' (*It's doubtful that he'll come*); with a person it means 'unsure' (*I'm doubtful about the plan*).

senses.gloss: Unlikely to happen or to be true.
examples: It's *doubtful* that the bill will pass this year.
His return this season looks *doubtful*.

senses.gloss: Not sure that something is right or will work.
examples: I'm *doubtful* about spending that much on a roof.
She sounded more *doubtful* the second time I asked.

contrast: A *doubting Thomas* is someone who won't believe anything until he sees proof.

senses.gloss: Showing that you do not believe or trust something.
examples: He gave me a *doubting* look and asked for the receipt.
Even the *doubting* neighbors showed up to see it.
Don't be such a *doubting* Thomas.

senses.gloss: Soft and undercooked inside, like raw dough.
examples: The middle of the loaf is still *doughy*.
That pizza came out *doughier* than the last one.

senses.gloss: Of a face or body: pale, soft and unhealthy-looking.
examples: He looked pale and *doughy* after a winter indoors.
A *doughy* man in a gray suit took our names.

contrast: Most Americans say /ˈdaʊər/, to rhyme with *hour*; /dʊr/ is also heard.

senses.gloss: Unfriendly and severe, showing no warmth or humor.
examples: The *dour* clerk didn't look up once.
He gets *dour* when the subject turns to money.
She's the most *dour* coach in the conference.

senses.gloss: Favoring peace and talks rather than force, or favoring low interest rates rather than tight money.
examples: She took a *dovish* line on the intervention.
The statement was more *dovish* than traders expected.
Two *dovish* members voted against the hike.

contrast: It is about dull, old-fashioned clothes, not about being ugly, and it is said almost only about women — so it stings.

senses.gloss: Dressed in dull, old-fashioned clothes.
examples: She felt *dowdy* next to the other guests.
The costume department made her look *dowdier* than she is.
He described the hotel as comfortable but *dowdy*.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *the system is down*
contrast: *Down* is mostly a preposition (*down the street*), an adverb (*sit down*), a verb and a noun. Only the meanings below work as adjectives. Note *a down payment*, where *down* is not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Sad or depressed.
examples: She's been *down* since the funeral.
I get a little *down* in February.

senses.gloss: Of a computer, network or machine: not working.
examples: The payment system is *down* again.
Their site was *down* for six hours.

senses.gloss: Lower in number or amount than before.
examples: Sales are *down* eight percent this quarter.
Gas prices are *down* from last summer.

senses.gloss: Losing by a certain amount in a game.
examples: We were *down* by two with a minute left.
They're *down* three games to one in the series.

position: predicative only — after *have* or *get* + object: *I have it down pat*
contrast: It follows the object, not the verb *be*: say *She has the routine down pat*, never *the routine is down pat*.

senses.gloss: Learned or practiced so well that you can do it perfectly every time.
examples: She has her opening line *down pat*.
After a week he had the espresso machine *down pat*.
Get the first ten measures *down pat* before you go on.

form: compound — the phrase *down and out* used as one adjective
contrast: Also a noun: *a shelter for the down-and-outs*. After a verb the hyphens usually drop: *He was down and out for a while*.

senses.gloss: Having no money, no job and nowhere to live.
examples: The diner fed *down-and-out* regulars for free.
He was *down and out* the winter after the plant closed.
It's a movie about a *down-and-out* boxer.

form: compound — the phrase *down to earth* used as one adjective
contrast: In English this is praise — sensible and unpretentious — while Russian *приземлённый* can sound like an insult.

senses.gloss: Practical, sensible and easy to talk to, with no airs.
senses.ru: простой в общении, без претензий; здравомыслящий
examples: For a famous actor, she's remarkably *down-to-earth*.
We need a *down-to-earth* plan, not a wish list.
He's the most *down-to-earth* person on the board.
